definition: Attributional calculus is a logic and representation system defined by Ryszard S.
details: Michalski. It combines elements of predicate logic, propositional calculus, and multi-valued logic. Attributional calculus provides a formal language for natural induction, which is an inductive learning process whose outcomes are in human-readable forms.

explainer.lead: Attributional calculus is a logical language for describing what an inductive learning system discovers in a form people can read. It matters because learned knowledge can then be inspected and discussed rather than left only as an opaque internal representation.

tiers.eli5: Imagine sorting fruit and then writing notes such as, “If it is yellow and curved, call it a banana.” Attributional calculus is a careful way of writing those notes, so a learning process can explain its conclusions with words and rules people understand.
tiers.practitioner: Use it as a representation layer when inductive learning must produce inspectable descriptions or rules. Its combination of predicate, propositional, and multi-valued logic supports richer expressions than plain yes-or-no propositions alone. Do not confuse the representation language with the induction procedure, or treat a readable learned rule as proof that it is accurate or causal.
tiers.paperLevel: Attributional calculus, defined by Ryszard S. Michalski, is a logic and representation system combining predicate logic, propositional calculus, and multi-valued logic. It supplies a formal language for natural induction: an inductive learning mapping from evidence to hypotheses expressed in human-readable form. The calculus represents the learned knowledge; natural induction is the learning process that produces it.

explainer.example: After learning from weather records, a system might express a readable rule such as: “If the outlook is sunny and humidity is high, then outdoor play is unsuitable.” Attributional calculus provides the kind of formal language used to represent such an inductive outcome.

usedIn.name: Natural induction
usedIn.detail: Provides the formal language in which human-readable inductive learning outcomes can be expressed.

usedIn.name: Inductive learning
usedIn.detail: Represents learned descriptions so people can inspect the results of learning.

usedIn.name: Knowledge representation
usedIn.detail: Combines several logical traditions to express learned knowledge symbolically.

explainer.intuition: A learning result is more useful when it can be stated as understandable knowledge rather than only as an internal score or parameter set. Attributional calculus supplies the logical vocabulary for writing that knowledge.
howItWorks: Describe objects and situations with logical statements.
Draw on predicate and propositional forms to express those statements.
Use multi-valued logic when description needs more than simple true-or-false values.
Apply the language within natural induction so learned outcomes take human-readable forms.
explainer.whyItMatters: It connects inductive learning with explicit symbolic representation, making learned conclusions available for human reading and examination. This separates the task of learning from the task of expressing what was learned.
misconceptions: It is not itself the natural induction learning procedure; it is the language used to represent that procedure’s outcomes.
It is not limited to propositional true-or-false statements, because it also incorporates predicate and multi-valued logic.
Human-readable output does not by itself guarantee that a learned conclusion is correct.

diagram.caption: Natural induction performs the learning, while attributional calculus supplies the logical language for its readable outcomes.
